def:
One of the measured gaps between consecutive protocol events of a single command in a capture (for example doorbell to SQE fetch, fetch to data, data to CQE, CQE to interrupt, interrupt to head doorbell), used to attribute latency to host, link or device.
Kid version: timing each leg of a relay race instead of only the whole race.
Where used: performance analysis of analyzer captures.
Common confusion: an interval names where time passed, not why; the cause still needs evidence.

The part of a test that decides whether data read back is correct, typically from a model of what was written and made durable plus a self-describing pattern (LBA, sequence, run ID, checksum) in each block.
Kid version: the answer key the teacher marks against.
Where used: storage validation, power-loss and reset testing.
Common confusion: an oracle can be wrong too; disagreements must be checked against the oracle's own model.

A property that must hold at every point of a correct protocol exchange (for example, a CQE never precedes the data it completes; a CID is not reused while outstanding), checked by scripts against traces or logs.
Kid version: a rule of the game that is never allowed to break.
Where used: validation rule engines, trace checkers.
Common confusion: a check that is true only in one implementation is not an invariant of the protocol.

A defect that passed all tests and was found later (by another team, a customer or in the field); escape analysis asks which test should have caught it and why it did not.
Kid version: a mistake that slipped past the spelling check.
Where used: validation process improvement.
Common confusion: the fix is to the test or oracle, not only to the product.

A written design for an analyzer capture: the question, the events and layers needed, probe points, trigger logic and pre-trigger share, filters and what each makes invisible, metadata to record, and the clock-anchoring method.
Kid version: deciding what to watch for before you start watching.
Where used: protocol-analyzer investigations, disputes between teams.
Common confusion: default settings plus a trigger is not a plan.

A TLP that appears twice on one link because the Data Link Layer retransmitted it with the same sequence number after a Nak or replay-timer expiry; the receiver discards copies it already accepted.
Kid version: the same letter sent twice because the first was smudged.
Where used: analyzer packet views, export processing.
Common confusion: counting it as a second transaction, for example a 'duplicate CQE'.

An analyzer export mapped onto a stable, vendor-neutral schema (time, direction, link, layer, type, requester, tag, address, length, sequence, status, payload prefix) with the capture's metadata attached, so scripts and rule engines can process it.
Kid version: copying everyone's notes into the same table.
Where used: automated trace analysis.
Common confusion: vendor column names and units differ and change between versions; never assume them.
